column1: OAuth Delegation Tokens for Agentic AI — Sub-Requirement Coverage [RFC-only baseline — 111 sub-requirements aligned on the draft]

✓ Covered = normative RFC text defines this sub-requirement    ◐ Partial = RFC text exists but leaves documented gaps    ✗ Gap = no normative RFC coverage — RFC contribution required    |    Note: R13 ◐ sub-point = authorization-time interaction only, does NOT satisfy R13 execution-time oversight

column3: Sub-requirement
column6: Justification (verified against RFC text)

column3: Define OAuth protocol roles (Resource Owner, Client, AS, Protected Resource)
column6: RFC 6749 §1.1 explicitly names and defines the four OAuth 2.0 protocol roles.
column7: No agent, delegate, or sub-agent roles are defined.

column3: Represent subject identity in access tokens
column6: RFC 9068 §2.2 defines sub as a mandatory JWT access token claim representing the principal that is the subject of the JWT.
column7: No semantics for software agent identity distinct from end-user or client identity.

column3: Represent the acting party in delegated execution
column6: RFC 8693 §4.1 defines the act claim to represent the entity acting on behalf of the subject. The claim value is a JSON object whose members identify the actor.
column7: No normative semantics for autonomous or ephemeral agent participants beyond the exchanger role.

column3: Represent chains of delegation actors
column4: • RFC 8693 §4.1 (nested act chain; prior actors informational per §4.1)
column6: RFC 8693 §4.1 permits nested act claims to represent a chain of delegation: each act object may itself contain an act member. The nesting structure is defined but no normative validation, depth limit, or chain-traversal procedure is specified.
column7: No normative ancestry validation. No depth limit. Nesting semantics are informative.

column3: Runtime retrieval of participant identity metadata
column4: • RFC 7662 §2.2 (active, scope, client_id, sub, aud, iss, jti) / • RFC 8693 §4.1 (act extensible to introspection response)
column6: RFC 7662 §2.2 defines the introspection response members: active, scope, client_id, username, token_type, exp, iat, nbf, sub, aud, iss, jti. The act claim is NOT defined by RFC 7662; it is defined by RFC 8693 §4.1 which states that act may appear as a top-level member of an introspection response with the same semantics. No participant discovery semantics for dynamic or multi-agent topologies are defined by either RFC.
column7: act in introspection is an extension defined by RFC 8693, not RFC 7662. No discovery semantics for dynamic agent topologies.

column3: Persistent or key-bound client/subject identity
column4: • RFC 9635 §11.10 (key-bound access tokens — GNAP protocol; not OAuth 2.0)
column6: RFC 9635 §11.10 defines key-bound access tokens in GNAP, where the access token is cryptographically bound to a key held by the client instance, providing persistent verifiable identity. Note: RFC 9635 is the GNAP core access protocol — not an OAuth 2.0 RFC. Coverage here is partial because: (a) GNAP is a separate authorization protocol; (b) RFC 9635 does not define ephemeral or sub-agent identity scoping.
column7: No persistent agent identity model in any OAuth 2.0 RFC.

column3: Ephemeral agent or sub-agent identity
column6: No OAuth RFC defines ephemeral delegates or sub-agents — participants existing only for the duration of a single task or invocation.

column3: Local vs. global scoping of participant identifiers
column4: • RFC 6749 §2.2 (client identifiers are unique to the authorization server; no global agent identifier model)
column6: No OAuth RFC defines whether agent or delegate identifiers are locally or globally scoped. RFC 8693 uses URI-form sub and act values by convention; no normative scoping semantics are imposed.

column3: Distinguish upstream from downstream delegation participants
column6: No OAuth RFC defines delegation participant lineage semantics. The nested act structure of RFC 8693 §4.1 does not normatively define upstream vs. downstream participant relationships or provide traversal rules.

column3: Distinguish delegated execution from unrestricted impersonation
column4: • RFC 8693 §1.1 (delegation vs. impersonation) / • RFC 8693 §4.1 (act claim) / • RFC 8693 §4.4 (may_act)
column6: RFC 8693 §1 explicitly defines delegation as distinct from impersonation. §4.4 introduces the may_act claim as the normative mechanism authorising a specific party to act on behalf of the subject, making the delegation explicit and permissioned.

column3: Represent the acting party separately from the subject
column4: • RFC 9068 §2.2 (sub — mandatory in JWT AT profile; identifies principal) / • RFC 8693 §4.1 (act — current actor performing delegated execution) / [Note: sub base definition is RFC 7519 §4.1.2, not in the 18-RFC corpus]
column6: Within the OAuth JWT access-token profile (RFC 9068 §2.2), sub is a mandatory claim identifying the principal on whose behalf authority is exercised. RFC 8693 §4.1 defines act as the entity currently performing delegated execution. The two claims are normatively separated. Note: the base JWT definition of sub is RFC 7519 §4.1.2, which is not part of the 18-RFC OAuth corpus evaluated here; RFC 9068 §2.2 is the appropriate OAuth-corpus reference.

column3: Prevent identity collapse in multi-hop delegation chains
column4: • RFC 8693 §4.1 (nested act — partial; prior actors informational only per §4.1)
column6: RFC 8693 §4.1 describes nested act claims as a mechanism to preserve actor identity across multiple hops. No normative rules mandate that downstream delegates preserve upstream act claims or prevent identity collapse through omission or overwriting.
column7: No normative multi-hop impersonation prevention. Chain integrity is not enforced.

column3: Preserve accountability across multiple delegation hops
column6: No RFC defines accountability semantics across multiple delegation hops. RFC 8693 act chain informally supports two-hop actor representation; no normative chain integrity requirements exist for longer chains.

column3: Scope-based restriction of delegated authority
column6: RFC 6749 §3.3 defines the scope parameter as a space-separated list of scope values restricting access. RFC 9068 §2.2 carries scope in the JWT access token.

column3: Audience restriction of delegated authority
column6: RFC 8707 §2 defines the resource parameter enabling AS to issue tokens restricted to specific resource URIs. RFC 9068 §2.2 mandates the aud claim.

column3: Structured, action-specific, resource-specific authorization constraints
column6: RFC 9396 §2 defines the authorization_details parameter as a JSON array of typed objects with fields type, actions, locations, and data_object, enabling structured constraints beyond scope strings.

column3: Narrowing of delegated authority during token exchange
column6: RFC 8693 §2.1 allows the scope parameter in a token exchange request to request narrower authority than the source token's scope. Narrowing is permitted but not mandated; no normative non-expansion enforcement mechanism exists.
column7: Non-expansion is informative, not normatively enforced by any RFC.

column3: Tool-invocation-level authorization constraints
column6: No RFC defines authorization semantics for specific tool invocations, API schemas, or agent tool calls. RFC 9396 authorization_details types are extensible but no normative type for tool-level agent constraints exists.
column7: Gap: requires new normative type definition under RFC 9396 extension or new spec.

column3: Workflow or transaction-scoped delegation constraints
column6: No OAuth RFC defines workflow-bound or transaction-scoped delegation. No normative mechanism binds delegated authority to a specific parent transaction or orchestration context.

column3: Guarantee of authority monotonicity (downstream authority cannot exceed upstream)
column6: No RFC normatively guarantees that downstream delegated authority cannot exceed upstream authority. RFC 8693 §2.1 notes the intent as a design consideration without mandating enforcement.
column7: Gap: requires new normative definition with enforcement mechanism.

column3: AS validates authorization requests (scope and authorization_details)
column6: RFC 6749 §3.3 requires the AS to validate the scope parameter. RFC 9396 §3 requires the AS to evaluate authorization_details at authorization time.

column3: RS validates access token and rejects insufficient authorization
column6: RFC 6750 §3 defines RS obligations: validate the token, verify scope sufficiency, return insufficient_scope or invalid_token as appropriate.

column3: AS as authoritative source of token active state
column6: RFC 7662 §2 defines the introspection endpoint through which the AS provides authoritative token state. RFC 6749 §5 defines the AS as the token issuer and lifecycle authority.

column3: Reject execution when authorization_details type is unknown
column6: RFC 9396 §5 states: 'The AS MUST refuse to process any unknown authorization details type or authorization details not conforming to the respective type definition' and MUST return invalid_authorization_details. This covers AS-side rejection of unknown authorization_details types. It does NOT cover rejection by non-AS actors (agent platforms, tool providers) of generic delegation constraints that are not expressed as authorization_details types.
column7: RFC 9396 §5 covers AS rejection of unknown authorization_details types only. No RFC defines rejection by agent platforms or tool providers of unrecognized delegation constraints.

column3: Designate a named enforcement actor for each delegation constraint type
column6: No RFC defines a mechanism for associating a specific delegation constraint with a named enforcement actor (AS, RS, Agent Platform, Tool Provider). RFC 9396 implies AS and RS but does not define per-constraint actor designation as a protocol construct.

column3: Define enforcement responsibilities across heterogeneous agent platforms
column6: No RFC defines enforcement responsibilities across agent platform boundaries. The agent platform role does not exist in the OAuth protocol model.

column3: Resource Owner role
column6: RFC 6749 §1.1 explicitly defines and names the Resource Owner protocol role.

column3: OAuth Client role
column6: RFC 6749 §1.1 explicitly defines and names the Client protocol role.

column3: Authorization Server role
column6: RFC 6749 §1.1 defines the AS role. RFC 8414 §2 defines AS metadata enabling interoperable discovery of AS capabilities.

column3: Protected Resource (Resource Server) role
column6: RFC 6749 §1.1 defines the Protected Resource role. RFC 9728 §2 defines Protected Resource metadata.

column3: Subject vs. actor distinction
column4: • RFC 9068 §2.2 (sub — mandatory JWT AT claim, entity on whose behalf authority is exercised) / • RFC 8693 §4.1 (act — entity performing delegated execution) / [Note: sub base definition is RFC 7519 §4.1.2, not in the 18-RFC corpus]
column6: Within the OAuth JWT access-token profile (RFC 9068 §2.2), sub is a mandatory claim identifying the entity on whose behalf authority is exercised. RFC 8693 §4.1 defines act as the entity performing delegated execution. The distinction is normative and explicitly stated. Note: RFC 7519 §4.1.2 is the base JWT definition of sub but is not part of the 18-RFC OAuth corpus; RFC 9068 §2.2 is the appropriate OAuth-corpus reference.

column3: Client instance vs. subject separation
column4: • RFC 9635 §11.10 (key-bound access tokens and client-instance binding — GNAP protocol; not OAuth 2.0)
column6: RFC 9635 §11.10 defines key-bound access tokens in GNAP, separating the client instance identity (cryptographic key) from the subject on whose behalf access is requested. This subject/client-instance separation is structurally analogous to the sub/act split in OAuth 2.0 delegation, but is defined within the GNAP protocol, not any OAuth 2.0 RFC. Coverage is ✓ for the conceptual distinction; GNAP-vs-OAuth scope difference reduces direct normative applicability to OAuth deployments.

column3: Delegator role (principal granting authority to a delegate)
column6: No RFC introduces 'delegator' as a named protocol role. RFC 8693 implicitly treats the subject_token presenter as the delegating party but defines no distinct delegator role with explicit semantics.

column3: Delegate agent role (software agent receiving and exercising delegated authority)
column6: No RFC defines a 'delegate agent' role for software agents acting autonomously. RFC 8693 defines 'actor' for the token exchanger; this partially overlaps but is not equivalent to an autonomous executing agent.

column3: Downstream delegation participant role
column6: No RFC defines downstream delegation participants as a named protocol role. RFC 8693 §4.1 describes nested act informally; no taxonomy of downstream participant roles is defined.

column3: Delegation ancestry semantics (upstream/downstream participant relationships)
column6: No RFC defines delegation ancestry semantics: traversal rules, chain validation, or the normative relationship between ancestor and descendant delegates.

column3: Expiration of the delegated token
column6: RFC 9068 §2.2 mandates the exp claim in JWT access tokens. §4 requires the RS to reject tokens where the current time exceeds exp.

column3: Active-state validation of token lifetime
column6: RFC 7662 §2.2 defines the active boolean in the introspection response. active:false indicates the token has expired, been revoked, or is otherwise invalid.

column3: Rejection of expired tokens by the Protected Resource
column6: RFC 6750 §3.1 defines the invalid_token error code returned by the RS for expired, revoked, or otherwise invalid tokens.

column3: Revocation as effective shortening of token lifetime
column6: RFC 7009 §2.1 defines the revocation endpoint. Revocation terminates a token's operational lifetime before its exp. RFC 7009 does not address this in the context of delegation chain lifetime constraints. Caveat: RFC 7009 §2.1 requires refresh-token revocation (MUST) but only SHOULD for access-token revocation — access-token revocation support is not universally guaranteed across all AS implementations.
column7: Revocation semantics are defined for individual tokens only, not for delegation chain lifetime constraints.

column3: Downstream delegation lifetime bounded by upstream (monotonic inheritance)
column6: No RFC defines monotonic lifetime inheritance. RFC 8693 does not define any normative relationship between source and derived token expiration; no normative rule requires derived_token.exp ≤ source_token.exp.

column3: Normative relationship between upstream and downstream lifetime constraints
column6: No RFC defines the normative relationship between upstream and downstream delegation lifetime constraints across a multi-hop chain.

column3: Renewal and reauthorization semantics for persistent delegation chains
column6: RFC 6749 defines the refresh_token grant, but no RFC defines renewal or reauthorization semantics specific to delegated authority that persists across multiple agentic execution contexts.

column3: Token revocation endpoint and protocol
column6: RFC 7009 §2 defines the revocation endpoint, request parameters, and normative AS obligations upon receiving a revocation request. RFC 7009 §2.1 MUST support refresh-token revocation; SHOULD support access-token revocation. Access-token revocation is not universally guaranteed across all OAuth AS implementations. No cascade or downstream propagation semantics are defined.

column3: Revocation state discovery by relying parties
column6: RFC 7662 §2.2 defines active:false as the normative signal for revoked, expired, or inactive tokens, enabling relying parties to discover revocation state via introspection.

column3: Rejection of revoked tokens by the Protected Resource
column6: RFC 6750 §3.1 defines invalid_token as the error response for revoked tokens presented to the RS.

column3: Cascading revocation to downstream delegation artifacts
column6: No RFC defines cascading revocation. RFC 7009 §2.1 mentions associated tokens only in the context of refresh/access token pairs under the same grant — not delegation chains. Revoking a source token via RFC 7009 has no normative effect on downstream tokens derived from it via RFC 8693.

column3: Subtree revocation (invalidating all tokens in a delegation subtree)
column6: No RFC defines subtree revocation semantics.

column3: Partial delegation revocation (revoking specific permissions without full token invalidation)
column6: No RFC defines partial delegation revocation. RFC 7009 operates at the token level, not the permission level.

column3: Revocation behavior during in-progress delegated execution
column6: No RFC defines the protocol behavior when a token is revoked while an agentic task using that token is actively executing.

column3: Revocation latency and consistency (immediate vs. eventual)
column4: • RFC 7662 (introspection; latency deployment-dependent — RS must call per-request for immediate detection) / • RFC 9068 (JWT bearer — eventual by default) / • RFC 7009 §2.1 (immediate AS invalidation, possible propagation delay; no bound)
column6: RFC 7662 token introspection enables revocation detection only when the RS calls introspection for each request — detection latency is deployment-specific and caching-dependent. Near-immediate detection is possible but not guaranteed by RFC 7662. RFC 9068 JWT bearer tokens validate locally; revocation is eventually consistent by default absent per-request introspection. No RFC defines normative latency requirements for revocation propagation.
column7: No normative revocation latency requirements or propagation guarantees defined.

column3: Freshness / availability declaration — maximum stale-authority window, means of bounding it, and failure mode (fail open / fail closed) when fresher state cannot be obtained
column6: Draft R6(i): stale-authority window, means of bounding it, and failure mode when fresher state cannot be obtained. RFC 7662 §2.2; §4: A+B, no C. A: normative upper bound on cached-state age (cache MUST NOT outlive exp) plus explicit discussion that cache timeout sets the revoked-token window; B: online introspection + bounded RS cache (§2.2 "MAY be cached"). No C: nothing says what the RS does when the introspection endpoint is unreachable; no mandated per-request/interval re-check.; RFC 7009 §2.1; §3; §5: A+B, no C. A (informative): short access-token lifetime limits the time a revoked token stays usable; §2.1 acknowledges a propagation-delay window and says "Implementations should minimize that window". B: lifetime, and §3 introspection-style AS/RS interaction for immediate revocation. No C: only client-side 503 retry (§2.2.1); nothing on RS behaviour when revocation state is unavailable.; RFC 6819 §3.2; §3.3; §5.1.5.3: A+B, no C. A (informative): short access-token lifetime bounds revocation latency (refresh-token revocation takes effect "once the current access token expires"); §3.2 "passive revocation ... on the expiry of the current access token". B: lifetime + refresh-token revocation. No C. Sections after 5.1.5.8 (5.2-5.4) unreadable (fetch cap).; RFC 9767 (GNAP) §3.3; §6.2; §6.3: B explicit (+A discussed, unbounded), no C. B: online introspection (§3.3), RS cache lifetime management, optional proactive AS signal (§6.3). A: window named as a cache-lifetime trade-off but no bound or interval stated. No C: RS behaviour when AS unreachable not addressed (§3.3 'discretion of the RS' concerns response choice). GNAP protocol, not OAuth 2.0.; RFC 9635 (GNAP) §6.2; §11.32; §11.33: A+B, no C. A (informative): short validity windows bound post-revocation usability of self-contained tokens; B: lifetime plus optional AS push of revoked-token identifiers (out of scope). No C. §11.32 lies beyond the rfc-editor fetch cap; quote verified against GitHub source draft-20 only. GNAP protocol, not OAuth 2.0.

column3: Access token validation (issuer, audience, validity period, subject, client identifier)
column6: RFC 9068 §4 defines a normative validation procedure: RS verifies iss against a trusted issuer list, validates aud contains the RS identifier, checks exp and nbf, and validates sub and client_id claims.

column3: Token active-state validation via introspection
column6: RFC 7662 §2 defines the normative introspection procedure. The active boolean is the primary validity indicator for relying parties using opaque tokens.

column3: Bearer token validation and error signaling at the RS
column6: RFC 6750 §3 defines the RS-side validation procedure for bearer tokens including the WWW-Authenticate challenge format and error codes invalid_token, insufficient_scope, and invalid_request.

column3: Sender-constrained token validation (DPoP and mTLS)
column4: • RFC 9449 §7 (DPoP proof validation) / • RFC 8705 §3 (mTLS cert-bound validation)
column6: RFC 9449 §7 defines normative DPoP proof validation at the RS including ath, nonce, htm, and htu checks. RFC 8705 §3 defines certificate-bound token validation using cnf.x5t#S256.

column3: Actor and authorized-actor validation
column6: RFC 8693 §4.1 defines the act claim structure and §4.4 defines may_act for restricting permitted actors. No normative validation procedure specifying how the RS verifies actor legitimacy or may_act compliance against the acting client is defined.
column7: No normative actor validation procedure at the RS is defined.

column3: Delegation ancestry validation across multi-hop chains
column6: No RFC defines a normative procedure for validating delegation ancestry. The nested act structure of RFC 8693 §4.1 is described but no validation rules for traversing or verifying the chain are specified.
column8: Derived ← R4 delegation ancestry semantics; R0 actor-chain representation

column3: Delegation-depth validation
column6: No RFC defines delegation depth limits or a normative validation procedure for enforcing them.

column3: Delegation provenance validation — authenticity and completeness of execution records, including tool invocations, state transitions and human approvals, consistent with delegated authority
column6: No RFC defines provenance validation across multiple delegation hops.
column8: Derived ← R12 execution and tool-invocation provenance

column3: Possession assumptions (whether possession alone suffices or authority is bound to keys, identities or contexts)
column4: • RFC 6750 §5 (bearer: possession sufficient, TLS required) / • RFC 7800 §3 (PoP key semantics) / • RFC 9449 §9; RFC 8705 §7 (key-bound artifacts)
column6: RFC 6750 §5 states that possession of a bearer token is sufficient and that TLS is required; RFC 7800 §3, RFC 9449 §9 and RFC 8705 §7 define the key-bound alternative.

column3: Presentation assumptions (how a presenter proves ownership or presents the artifact; presentation recommendations)
column4: • RFC 9449 §9 (DPoP proof presentation) / • RFC 8705 §7 (mTLS client authentication of the presenter) / • RFC 9700 (BCP 240 — presentation recommendations)
column6: RFC 9449 and RFC 8705 define how a presenter proves possession when presenting the artifact, and RFC 9700 (BCP 240) gives the security recommendations for presentation.

column3: Transfer and forwarding assumptions (transmission across entity boundaries, protection in transit, recursive forwarding)
column6: RFC 6750 §5 requires TLS for bearer token transmission, which covers protection in transit. No RFC defines rules for transmitting an artifact across entity boundaries in a multi-agent system or for recursive forwarding to downstream agents.
column7: Partial: protection in transit only; no forwarding rules.

column3: Storage and disclosure assumptions (storage, processing, logging, retention, selective disclosure)
column6: RFC 9901 §11 defines SD-JWT security considerations including holder binding and selective disclosure integrity. No RFC defines requirements for how delegation artifacts are stored, processed, logged, retained or disclosed in autonomous or multi-agent execution.
column7: Partial: selective disclosure of one artifact format only.

column3: Replay assumptions (inherent replay resistance or external controls)
column4: • RFC 9449 §9 (DPoP replay resistance) / • RFC 6750 §5 (bearer: no inherent replay resistance, TLS required)
column6: RFC 9449 §9 defines the replay-resistance properties of DPoP-bound tokens, and RFC 6750 §5 states that a bearer token has no inherent replay resistance and relies on TLS.

column3: Derivation and re-delegation assumptions (derivation, recursion limits, no authority expansion)
column6: No RFC defines normative constraints on deriving new delegation artifacts from existing delegated authority. RFC 8693 defines token exchange as one derivation mechanism but does not restrict recursive derivation or prevent authority expansion.

column3: Audience and context restrictions (target components, tool schemas, parent transactions, runtime environments)
column6: RFC 9068 §2.2 mandates aud and RFC 8707 §2 lets the client indicate the target resource; this restricts validity to target components only. No RFC restricts an artifact to tool schemas, parent transactions or runtime environments.
column7: Component/audience restriction only; no tool-schema, transaction or runtime-environment restriction.

column3: Security consequences of artifact compromise (blast radius, failures, remediation, chains across trust domains)
column6: No RFC defines blast radius or remediation behavior specific to compromised delegation chain artifacts. RFC 7009 defines revocation but not in the context of chain-wide compromise remediation.

column3: Proof-of-possession key semantics and key-confirmation binding
column6: RFC 7800 §3 defines the cnf (confirmation) claim and associated key binding semantics for JWTs, establishing the normative foundation for PoP in the JWT/OAuth space.

column3: Application-layer sender-constrained tokens (DPoP)
column6: RFC 9449 §4 defines DPoP proof JWT structure. §7 defines the normative RS-side validation procedure for sender-constrained tokens including ath, nonce, htm, and htu verification.

column3: Transport-layer sender-constrained tokens (mTLS certificate binding)
column6: RFC 8705 §3 defines certificate-bound access tokens using cnf.x5t#S256 and the normative mTLS validation procedure at the RS.

column3: Verifier designation and validation requirements
column4: • RFC 9449 §7 (RS verifies DPoP) / • RFC 8705 §3 (RS validates cert)
column6: RFC 9449 §7 and RFC 8705 §3 both explicitly designate the RS as the verifier responsible for validating the binding proof.

column3: Replay resistance for bound tokens
column6: RFC 9449 §8.1 defines nonce-based replay resistance and jti uniqueness requirements for DPoP proofs, preventing replay attacks.

column3: Runtime or workload-context binding
column6: No OAuth RFC defines binding of delegated authority to a specific runtime workload, execution environment, or agent instance. SPIFFE SVIDs (informative prior art) provide workload identity but are outside the OAuth corpus.

column3: Rotation and failure behavior for binding credentials — replacing a compromised or expired binding credential (DPoP key pair, mTLS certificate) without invalidating the delegation chain
column6: No published OAuth RFC defines rotation or failure behavior for binding credentials in the context of delegation chains (draft R9(g)).

column3: Scope narrowing during token exchange
column4: • RFC 6749 §3.3 / • RFC 8693 §2.1 (scope narrowing in exchange request)
column6: RFC 6749 §3.3 defines scope as a restriction mechanism. RFC 8693 §2.1 allows a token exchange request to include a narrower scope than the source token. Narrowing is permitted but not mandated, and enforcement is not specified.
column7: Narrowing is permitted, not mandated. No normative enforcement mechanism.

column3: Structured authorization narrowing via authorization_details
column6: RFC 9396 §2 authorization_details objects can represent narrower permissions. No normative rule mandates that derived authorization_details cannot exceed the source's permissions. RFC 9396 explicitly states that authorization_details field semantics are defined per-type by each protected resource; there is no standardized mechanism to compare arbitrary authorization_details structures. Monotonic narrowing (downstream ≤ upstream) cannot be proved from RFC 9396 alone without additional specification.
column7: No attenuation mandate or verification mechanism for authorization_details.

column3: Formal attenuation algebra (normative rules for deriving downstream from upstream authority)
column6: No RFC defines a formal attenuation algebra or normative derivation rules for delegation authority chains. This is the core attenuation gap.

column3: Monotonic attenuation guarantee (downstream ≤ upstream)
column6: No RFC provides a normative monotonic attenuation guarantee. RFC 8693 §2.1 notes the intent as a design consideration; no enforcement mechanism exists.

column3: Verifiable proof that downstream authority is bounded by upstream authority
column6: No RFC defines a mechanism enabling a relying party to verify that a downstream delegation artifact's authority is a subset of its upstream artifact.

column3: Authority aggregation / co-delegation — whether one artifact may draw authority from several delegators; per-contributor bounding, attribution and verification
column4: • RFC 9767 §2.1.13; §4 (GNAP protocol; not OAuth 2.0) / • RFC 9635 §4 (GNAP protocol; not OAuth 2.0)
column6: No published OAuth RFC defines whether one delegation artifact may aggregate authority from several delegators, nor per-contributor bounding, attribution or verification (draft R10(f)). RFC 9767 (GNAP) §2.1.13; §4: Token model explicitly admits a set of ROs approving ONE grant/token (whether: yes); no bounding/attribution/verification per RO. §4 derived token 'issued in the context of the incoming access token' (single parent). GNAP protocol, not OAuth 2.0.; RFC 9635 (GNAP) §4: Explicitly permits one grant to require authorization from several ROs (nurse and physician; both owners of a bank account; N of M); which ROs are required and how is declared implementation-specific; permissive, not normative. GNAP protocol, not OAuth 2.0.

column3: Token transformation enabling authority propagation
column6: RFC 8693 §1 defines token exchange as a mechanism through which one security token may be exchanged for another, enabling one form of authority propagation. RFC 8693 does not define this as re-delegation or provide re-delegation permission/prohibition semantics.
column7: Token exchange ≠ re-delegation. No re-delegation semantics defined.

column3: Actor chain representation for multi-hop exchange
column6: RFC 8693 §4.1 describes nested act claims to represent chains of delegation through multiple exchange operations. No normative validation, depth constraints, or chain integrity rules are defined.
column7: Informative description only. No normative chain semantics.

column3: Explicit permission to re-delegate
column6: No RFC defines an explicit permission mechanism enabling a delegate to sub-delegate authority. There is no normative claim, policy mechanism, or protocol field for re-delegation permission.

column3: Explicit prohibition of re-delegation
column6: No RFC defines a normative mechanism for prohibiting re-delegation. A holder of a token obtained via RFC 8693 exchange is not prevented from performing a further exchange.

column3: Delegation depth limits
column6: No RFC defines a maximum delegation depth or a normative max_depth claim or equivalent.

column3: Downstream authority inheritance rules for re-delegated tokens
column6: No RFC defines normative rules governing how a re-delegated token's authority relates to its upstream token's authority.

column3: Delegation provenance — chain of custody of the authorization artifact across actors (per-token audit metadata; nested actor history)
column4: • RFC 9068 §2.2 (iss, sub, iat, jti) / • RFC 8693 §4.1 (nested act chain as actor history — informative; prior actors excluded from access control per §4.1)
column6: RFC 9068 §2.2 defines iss, sub, iat and jti as mandatory JWT access token claims (per-token audit metadata). RFC 8693 §4.1 describes nested act claims as a way to carry actor history across exchange operations, but this description is informative only; no normative chain integrity, verification or traversal procedure is defined.
column7: Per-token metadata covered; actor history across hops informative only. No normative chain provenance or integrity semantics.

column3: Runtime retrieval of provenance metadata
column4: • RFC 7662 §2.2 (iss, sub, client_id, jti in introspection) / • RFC 8693 §4.1 (act extensible to introspection)
column6: RFC 7662 §2.2 defines the introspection response members including iss, sub, client_id, and jti. The act claim is defined by RFC 8693 §4.1 as an extension to the introspection response — it is NOT part of RFC 7662's normative member list. No participant discovery semantics for dynamic multi-agent topologies are defined.
column7: act in introspection is RFC 8693 extension, not RFC 7662. No multi-agent topology discovery semantics.

column3: Execution provenance — state transitions, platform configurations and environments of the agent (linking delegated authority to security-relevant execution events)
column6: No RFC defines execution provenance for agentic systems.

column3: Invocation provenance — logging of explicit requests initiated by intermediary orchestration components
column6: No published OAuth RFC defines logging or recording of explicit requests initiated by intermediary orchestration components (draft R12(d)).

column3: Tool invocation provenance — parameters, schemas and API endpoints called under delegated authority
column6: No RFC defines provenance semantics for tool invocations performed under delegated authority.

column3: Human approval provenance (verifiable attestations of oversight decisions)
column6: No RFC defines provenance semantics for human oversight decisions during delegated execution.

column3: Provenance disclosure semantics (verifiability, mutability, selective disclosure, privacy)
column6: No RFC defines a provenance disclosure framework for delegation chains. RFC 9901 SD-JWT provides selective disclosure for individual JWT claims but not a chain-provenance disclosure model.

column3: End-user interaction during OAuth authorization
column4: • RFC 6749 §4.1 (authorization code flow)  • RFC 9635 §2 (GNAP interaction model)
column6: RFC 6749 §4.1 defines the authorization code flow including end-user interaction via the authorization endpoint at authorization time. RFC 9635 §2 defines GNAP's interaction model. R13(a) asks how authorization-time interaction is supported, which these mechanisms define. Execution-time human oversight is covered by R13(b)–(i), which no RFC defines.

column3: Human approval checkpoints during delegated execution
column6: No RFC defines protocol mechanisms for human approval checkpoints within a running delegated execution flow.

column3: Semantics of approval denial, interruption, or override during execution
column6: No RFC defines protocol-level effects of a human denying, interrupting, or overriding a delegated execution in progress.

column3: Human oversight policies (who is authorized to approve, trigger conditions)
column6: No RFC defines authorization semantics for human oversight providers or the conditions under which human involvement is required.

column3: Classification of delegated actions as autonomous vs. supervised
column6: No RFC defines a mechanism to classify delegated actions as requiring human supervision or permitting autonomous execution.

column3: Binding of a human approval to the exact delegated action and its parameters (what is approved is what is executed)
column6: No RFC defines binding of a human approval to the exact action and parameters executed.

column3: Approval validity window and invalidation when the action, parameters or context change between approval and execution (TOCTOU)
column6: No RFC defines an approval validity window or invalidation of an approval when the action, parameters or context change.

column3: Approver unavailability — substitution, delegation of approval authority, multi-party approval, and behavior when no valid approval is obtained
column6: No RFC defines approver substitution, delegation of approval authority, multi-party approval, or behavior when no valid approval is obtained.

column3: Control of approval request volume, grouping and presentation (approval fatigue)
column6: No RFC defines control of approval request volume, grouping or presentation.

column3: Bearer token error responses (invalid_token, insufficient_scope, invalid_request)
column6: RFC 6750 §3.1 defines the normative error taxonomy for bearer token failures including WWW-Authenticate challenge format and error codes.

column3: Expired, revoked or inactive delegated authority — failure signaling (error responses RFC 6750 §3.1; introspection active:false RFC 7662 §2.2)
column6: RFC 7662 §2.2 defines active:false as the normative failure signal for expired, revoked, or inactive tokens.

column3: Token exchange failure responses
column6: RFC 8693 §2.2 defines normative error responses for token exchange failures.

column3: Authorization-details failure handling
column4: • RFC 9396 §5 (invalid_authorization_details at AS) / • RFC 9396 §8 (token request failure)
column6: RFC 9396 §5 defines invalid_authorization_details for unknown or malformed types at AS authorization time. §7 defines token request failure. No normative failure mechanism exists for authorization_details constraint violations detected at execution time by agent platforms or tool providers.
column7: No execution-time constraint violation failure semantics defined.

column3: Delegation ancestry validation failure semantics
column6: No RFC defines failure semantics for delegation ancestry validation failures. Since ancestry validation is not defined in any RFC, its failure semantics cannot exist.

column3: Binding or proof-of-possession validation failures
column4: • RFC 9449 §7.1 (invalid_dpop_proof; §9 use_dpop_nonce at the RS) / • RFC 8705 §3 (RS MUST refuse a certificate-bound token when the certificate does not match)
column6: RFC 9449 defines DPoP error responses and RFC 8705 §3 the RS behavior when the bound certificate does not match; covered in part (per draft R14(f) wording). No failure semantics for binding failures within a delegation chain (downstream effect, observability).
column7: Single-token binding failures only; no chain-level consequence.

column3: Unauthorized re-delegation or delegation-depth violations — structural violations of the delegation chain (re-delegation without permission; depth exceeding the limit)
column6: No published OAuth RFC defines failure semantics for unauthorized re-delegation or delegation-depth violations (draft R14(g)).
column7: Gap: requires new normative definition; derived from R11 gaps.
column8: Derived ← R11 re-delegation permission/prohibition and depth limits

column3: Human approval failure semantics (behavior when required human oversight is unavailable)
column6: No RFC defines failure semantics for unavailable or denied human approval. Human oversight is entirely absent from the OAuth protocol model.
column8: Derived ← R13 approval checkpoints and denial semantics (R13.2, R13.3)
